newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Mediator says time running out for Yugo succession.
newsitem.headline: Mediator says time running out for Yugo succession.

text.p: An international mediator warned former Yugoslav republics on Saturday that time was running out for an agreement on the legal succession to the former federation.
"We are inching our way forward. But I am conscious now that we may be running out of time," Sir Arthur Watts told Reuters.

The talks on succession, which includes the division of former Yugoslavia's assets and liabilities, have been deadlocked for almost five years and are a major obstacle to establishing full relations between the five successors.
"The succession issue is in fact the international equivalent of the liquidation of a big multinational company," Watts said.
Following the signing of the Dayton peace accord for Bosnia, the international community decided to revive the succession talks, which had collapsed in 1994.
Watts, who was appointed special negotiator in March 1996, said the five states had established a framework for the technical and political complexities of the problem.
"I do not expect any delegation to surrender completely to the others. But they all must compromise further if there is to be any agreement," he added.
Yugoslavia, comprising the republics of Serbia and Montenegro, insists it is the only successor to the old federation, claiming that the other four republics broke away unconstitutionally.
Watts said he could not regard the negotiations as two-sided -- Belgrade against the other four.

"In the context of succession, the four states have a similar approach on many issues in principle. But there are many issues particularly on points of details where each delegation pursues its own national interest," he said.
There was nothing the ex-Yugoslav federal republics of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia and Yugoslavia were avoiding in the talks, but there were technically and politically difficult issues.
Watts saw defining the state property, access to the archives and the final distribution as the key issues on which the five parties held opposing views.
After two days of "encouraging" talks in Belgrade, Watts appealed on all sides to make only a small step, a token, to show the process can produce practical results.
He saw no alternative to international mediation and said it was unrealistic and unreasonable to expect the five states to sit and negotiate the issues themselves.

Watts was preparing a third draft of the memorandum of understanding for the end of July. He expected the next round of bilateral talks by mid-September and a plenary meeting at the beginning of October.
"My next draft will not be an unanimous agreement, but I hope just another step forward," he said.
Watts visited the Slovenian, Bosnian and Macedonian capitals earlier and was on his way to the Croatian capital Zagreb for another round of bilateral talks.
